description: SPHEREx Motion Finder by Naylamp Space es una herramienta web interactiva de ciencia ciudadana que permite a cualquier usuario explorar el universo en tiempo real. Mediante la animación de imágenes infrarrojas en serie temporal capturadas por la misión SPHEREx de la NASA, la plataforma facilita la detección visual de asteroides, cometas, estrellas variables y enanas marrones a través del análisis de su movimiento y variabilidad.
summary:
GALAC ONE is an astronomical data exploration platform developed by Naylamp Space for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge “Planet X and SPHEREx.” It uses infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission to help identify and investigate unusual astronomical sources, including objects that may exhibit unexpected movement, variability, or exceptionally red infrared signatures.

The platform combines automated image analysis, spectral subtraction, candidate detection, and citizen science. It allows users to explore potential objects and contribute to their classification, helping prioritize candidates for further scientific investigation.

GALAC ONE addresses the challenge by transforming large volumes of infrared astronomical data into accessible and actionable information. Its importance lies in making astronomical exploration more collaborative and accessible while supporting the search for unusual objects that could provide valuable clues about the outer Solar System. Although it does not claim to detect or confirm Planet X, it provides tools to investigate potential candidates and encourage scientific discovery.
details:
What it does and how it works

GALAC ONE is a citizen-science platform built on NASA SPHEREx data for the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge. SPHEREx photographs each patch of sky many times, each time at a different wavelength, so simply comparing two images makes every star appear to change and hides the few objects that really move or blink. A distant Planet X or a cold brown dwarf would be faint, red and slow. GALAC ONE solves this in three steps:

  • Removes what does not change: for every pixel we fit the star's own spectrum across all exposures and subtract it, leaving only movers, variables and artifacts.
  • Searches the sky by itself: an automatic crawler reads SPHEREx frames from NASA's public S3 bucket, aligns and stacks them (drizzle) region by region starting along the ecliptic, and looks for sources much redder than stars (cold-dwarf colours).
  • Lets people decide: candidates go to a one-screen game (Spot check, Follow a star, Sky hunt). Hidden test injections and empty-sky controls measure each player's reliability, and a weighted consensus (at least 3 people, 60% majority) decides what becomes a lead and what is ruled out.

Results with SPHEREx data alone

  • Barnard's Star proper motion: 10.10 ± 0.12″/yr (Gaia: 10.39″/yr, direction within 0.3°).
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.70 ± 0.06″/yr (Gaia: 4.68″/yr).
  • R Draconis: 238-day period, ~1.1 mag amplitude; RW Aurigae irregular variability detected.
  • WISE 0855 recovered blind: the only one of 19 red sources with a Y-dwarf spectrum, and the only one that moves.
  • Spectral subtraction removes static structure ×55 on a synthetic sky and ×4.5 on real stars; 82–90% of injected movers recovered above S/N 7; deep stacks reduce noise ×6–28.

Benefits and intended impact

GALAC ONE turns a huge spectral survey into something anyone can explore from a browser, with no account or installation. It multiplies the eyes looking for moving and changing objects in the infrared sky, produces vetted candidate lists for professional follow-up, and teaches students and the public how real astronomical discovery works: measurement, error bars and verification. Automatic candidates are presented honestly as leads, not discoveries, until they are cross-matched with other catalogues.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite and TypeScript, with Aladin Lite (CDS) as the sky viewer over IRSA's SPHEREx HiPS map.
  • Backend: Cloudflare Workers, D1 (votes, users, consensus) and R2 (field files).
  • Science pipeline: Python 3.11 (indexing from FITS headers, alignment, spectral subtraction, detection, proper motion, light curves, drizzle stacks, HiPS mosaics).
  • Automation and data: GitHub Actions for the sky crawler and a public Hugging Face dataset as the deep-sky data layer. Everything runs on free tiers. Open source under the MIT license.

Creativity

Instead of comparing images directly, we use each star's own spectrum as its model, which turns SPHEREx's changing wavelengths from an obstacle into an advantage. We combine an autonomous search of the whole sky with a game whose scoring is honest by design: hidden injections are never revealed by the API, so the community's answers are weighted by measured accuracy.

Factors we considered

Scientific rigour (every result validated against Gaia and synthetic injections, with unverified points documented), accessibility (one-screen game, keyboard shortcuts, no sign-up), privacy (anonymous votes with a random browser id, no keys in the browser), zero cost and reproducibility (free tiers and open code), and the limits of computing resources: the crawler ran every two hours until 15 November 2026 and is now paused until it moves to a host meant for long computations, while everything already stacked remains live.
